meaning: Every token scores every token (query · key), turns the scores into weights with softmax, and takes a weighted blend of their values. One step connects any two tokens and runs in parallel, unlike an RNN.

Three learned projections of each token: the query says what it is looking for, the key what it offers, the value what it hands over if picked. Q = XW<sub>Q</sub>, K = XW<sub>K</sub>, V = XW<sub>V</sub>.

softmax(QKᵀ / √d<sub>k</sub>) V. The division by √d<sub>k</sub> keeps scores near unit size: dot products of d-dimensional random vectors have variance d, and big scores make softmax one-hot with tiny gradients.

Sets every score where the key comes after the query to −∞ before softmax, so each token only sees itself and earlier tokens. Lets a decoder train all next-token predictions in one pass without peeking.
The n × n table of attention weights for one head: row = the token looking, column = the token looked at. Its size grows with the square of the sequence length.

Self-attention computes n² scores per head and layer, so doubling the context quadruples the work and the memory for the attention maps. FlashAttention avoids storing them; long-context methods reduce the work.

Runs h attentions in parallel on slices of size d/h, each with its own Q/K/V projections, then concatenates them and mixes with W<sub>O</sub>. Same 4d² weights as one wide head, h different patterns per token.
One of the parallel attentions in a multi-head layer, typically 64 or 128 numbers wide. Heads often specialize (previous token, determiner → noun, coreference); many can be pruned after training.
The d × d matrix applied after concatenating all heads' outputs, mixing them back into the model width.
Removing attention heads from a trained model. 2019 studies removed 20–40% of heads with no noticeable loss, and 38 of 48 encoder heads for a 0.15 BLEU drop in one translation model.
Any way of telling a transformer where each token sits, needed because self-attention is permutation-blind: shuffle the words and each token gets the same vector.
A trained table with one vector per position, added to the token embedding (BERT: 512 rows, GPT-2: 1,024). Simple, but there is no row past the trained length.

The 2017 Transformer's fixed position code: each dimension pair is sin/cos of pos / 10000<sup>2i/d</sup>, clock hands turning at geometric speeds. No parameters, but it extrapolates weakly in practice.
Put the distance between query and key into the attention score instead of giving tokens absolute addresses (Shaw et al. 2018: +1.3 BLEU on English→German).
Rotates each 2D pair of a query by position × frequency and each key the same way, so q·k depends only on their distance. No parameters; used by Llama 3, Qwen3 and Gemma 3 (2024–25).
Attention with Linear Biases: no position vectors, just a penalty proportional to query–key distance added to each score (a slope per head). Designed to extrapolate to longer inputs; used by BLOOM.
Attention (mix across tokens) followed by an MLP (per token), each wrapped in a residual connection and a normalization. About 12d² weights per block with a 4× GELU MLP.
The per-token two-layer network inside each block: widen to about 4d, bend (ReLU, GELU or SwiGLU), shrink back to d. Holds about two thirds of a transformer's parameters.
The running sum x that flows through a transformer: every sublayer reads a normalized copy and adds its output back, nothing overwrites it. Gives gradients a slope-1 path to the bottom.

Post-norm (2017) normalizes after each residual add: bounded stream, but large gradients near the output at init, so it needs warm-up. Pre-norm (GPT-2 onward) normalizes each sublayer's input: clean residual path, trains without warm-up, needs a final norm.
Using the same V × d table for the input embedding and the output (unembedding) layer, saving V × d parameters (31% of GPT-2 small).
A transformer stack with no mask: every token sees both sides. Best for understanding a fixed text: classification, tagging, embeddings for search (BERT, ModernBERT).
A transformer stack with the causal mask, trained to predict the next token; generates text one token at a time (GPT, Llama, Qwen). The dominant design for general-purpose LLMs.
An encoder reads the source with full attention; a decoder writes the target with causal attention plus cross-attention to the encoder (original Transformer, T5, Whisper).
Attention where queries come from one sequence (the decoder) and keys and values from another (the encoder output). The transformer version of Bahdanau attention.
Always picking the most likely next token. Deterministic, but can fall into repetition loops; sampling with a temperature adds variety.
Turns text into integer ids from a fixed vocabulary of pieces (and back). A model only works with the exact tokenizer it was trained with.
Builds a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in the training text; tokenizes by applying the merges in order (Sennrich et al. 2015).
BPE over UTF-8 bytes (a base vocabulary of 256), so any string can be encoded and nothing is ever unknown; rare characters just cost several tokens (GPT-2, Qwen3).
BERT's subword algorithm: like BPE, but merges the pair with the best count-of-pair ÷ (count of each part) score. Word-internal pieces are marked “##”.
SentencePiece is a library that trains BPE or Unigram on raw text, treating the space as a symbol (“▁”). Unigram starts from a big vocabulary and prunes the least useful pieces (T5, Gemma).
The number of distinct tokens. Bigger means shorter sequences but a bigger embedding table and output layer: GPT-2 50,257; Llama 3 128K; Qwen3 151,669; Gemma 3 262k.
